# SYCL Programming Guide: Migrating CUDA Code
# Source: Data Parallel C++ (Reinders et al., Springer 2023), Chapter 21

CHAPTER 21 Migrating CUDA Code Many readers of this book have likely encountered data parallel code written in CUDA. Some readers may even be CUDA experts! In this chapter we will describe some of the similarities between CUDA and SYCL, some of the differences, and useful tools and techniques to help migrate CUDA code effectively and efficiently to C++ with SYCL. Design Differences Between CUDA and SYCL Before we dive into the details, it is first instructive to identify key design differences between CUDA and SYCL. This can provide useful background to inform why some differences exist, to understand which differences may disappear in time and which differences are likely to remain. Multiple Targets vs. Single Device Targets One of the biggest design differences between CUDA and SYCL is the universe of devices they are designed to support. CUDA is designed to support GPU devices from a single device vendor, so most CUDA devices look relatively similar. As an example, all CUDA devices currently include texture sampling hardware and all CUDA devices currently support the same maximum work-group size. This reduces complexity, but also reduces where a CUDA application may run. © Intel Corporation 2023 J. Reinders et al., Data Parallel C++, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4842-9691-2_21 580 By contrast, SYCL is designed to support a diverse set of heterogeneous accelerators, including different devices from different device vendors. This flexibility gives SYCL programs the freedom to take advantage of the computing resources in a modern heterogeneous system; however, this flexibility does come at a modest cost. For example, as SYCL programmers we may need to enumerate the devices in the system, examine their properties, and choose which device or devices are best suited to run different parts of our program. Of course, if our SYCL program does not intend to utilize all the computing resources in our system, various shortcuts exist to reduce code verbosity, such as standard device selectors. ## Key SYCL 2020 concepts for translating CUDA C++ to SYCL C++ for Intel GPUs with `icpx`

### CUDA-to-SYCL terminology mapping

- CUDA kernel → SYCL kernel
- CUDA thread → SYCL work-item
- CUDA block → SYCL work-group
- CUDA grid → SYCL ND-range
- CUDA warp → SYCL sub-group
- CUDA shared memory → SYCL local memory
- CUDA stream → SYCL queue
- `__syncthreads()` → `sycl::group_barrier()`
- `threadIdx`, `blockIdx`, `blockDim`, `gridDim` → `sycl::nd_item` queries

---

## Queue and device setup

SYCL uses a `sycl::queue` to submit kernels and memory operations to a device. A queue is roughly analogous to a CUDA stream.

For Intel GPUs with oneAPI/DPC++:

```cpp
sycl::queue q{sycl::gpu_selector_v};
```

or, to mimic CUDA stream ordering:

```cpp
sycl::queue q{
    sycl::gpu_selector_v,
    sycl::property::queue::in_order{}
};
```

CUDA streams are in-order by default. SYCL queues are out-of-order by default unless created with `property::queue::in_order`.

A typical Intel GPU build uses:

```bash
icpx -fsycl source.cpp -o app
```

Device selection can also be controlled at runtime, for example:

```bash
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:gpu ./app
```

Common device query:

```cpp
std::cout << q.get_device().get_info<sycl::info::device::name>() << "\n";
```

---

## Memory model and USM

SYCL supports Unified Shared Memory, which is often the closest migration path from CUDA pointer-based code.

### `malloc_device`

Closest to `cudaMalloc`.

```cpp
int* d_ptr = sycl::malloc_device<int>(n, q);
```

- Memory resides on the device.
- Host cannot directly dereference it.
- Use `q.memcpy`, kernels, or explicit copies.

CUDA equivalent:

```cpp
cudaMalloc(&ptr, n * sizeof(int));
```

SYCL equivalent:

```cpp
int* ptr = sycl::malloc_device<int>(n, q);
```

### `malloc_shared`

Similar in spirit to CUDA managed memory.

```cpp
int* ptr = sycl::malloc_shared<int>(n, q);
```

- Accessible by both host and device.
- Easier to port pointer-heavy CUDA code.
- May have migration or performance costs depending on access pattern.
- On Intel GPUs, behavior depends on the backend, platform, and memory system.

### `malloc_host`

Pinned host-accessible allocation associated with a SYCL context.

```cpp
int* ptr = sycl::malloc_host<int>(n, q);
```

- Host-accessible.
- Useful for efficient transfers.
- Similar in purpose to `cudaMallocHost`.

### Copies and initialization

CUDA:

```cpp
cudaMemcpy(dst, src, bytes, cudaMemcpyDefault);
cudaMemset(ptr, 0, bytes);
```

SYCL:

```cpp
q.memcpy(dst, src, bytes).wait();
q.memset(ptr, 0, bytes).wait();
```

or for typed values:

```cpp
q.fill(ptr, value, count).wait();
```

### Freeing USM

```cpp
sycl::free(ptr, q);
```

USM allocations are associated with a SYCL context. Avoid mixing allocations, queues, and devices from unrelated contexts.

---

## Kernel dispatch

CUDA launches kernels using special syntax:

```cpp
kernel<<<numBlocks, threadsPerBlock>>>(args);
```

SYCL uses standard C++ calls and lambdas.

### Simple 1D kernel

```cpp
q.parallel_for(sycl::range<1>{n}, [=](sycl::id<1> i) {
    ptr[i] = i;
}).wait();
```

### Explicit submission with `q.submit`

```cpp
q.submit([&](sycl::handler& h) {
    h.parallel_for(sycl::range<1>{n}, [=](sycl::id<1> i) {
        ptr[i] = i;
    });
}).wait();
```

`q.submit` is needed when using accessors, local memory, dependencies, or more complex command-group setup.

### ND-range kernel

CUDA:

```cpp
kernel<<<numBlocks, threadsPerBlock>>>(ptr);
```

SYCL:

```cpp
q.parallel_for(
    sycl::nd_range<1>{
        sycl::range<1>{numBlocks * threadsPerBlock},
        sycl::range<1>{threadsPerBlock}
    },
    [=](sycl::nd_item<1> item) {
        size_t gid = item.get_global_id(0);
        size_t lid = item.get_local_id(0);
        size_t group = item.get_group(0);
    }
